code.source:
words = ["fish", "crab", "fig", "fish"]
letters = {w[0] for w in words}
print(sorted(letters))
print(len(letters))

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: duplicate keys overwrite
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We use the first letter as the key. Fish and fig both start with f. The second one overwrites the first. Our dictionary has only two pairs, and fish is lost. No error, only missing data. Pick a key that is unique, like the whole word, and nothing is lost.

props.why: Two words with the same first letter make the same key, and the later pair replaces the earlier one, so one word is lost.

shorts.title: Dictionary comprehension
shorts.hook: "A dictionary comprehension builds a dictionary in one line."
shorts.script: A dictionary comprehension builds a dictionary in one line. Curly brackets, a key, a colon, a value, then for, the item, in, the source. Names to lengths becomes n, colon, len of n, for n in names. It is the same idea as a list comprehension, with curly brackets and a colon. Use it to turn one list into a lookup table. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Lookup tables in one line.

shorts.title: Set comprehension
shorts.hook: "A set comprehension looks like a dictionary one, but with no colon."
shorts.script: A set comprehension looks like a dictionary one, but with no colon. Curly brackets, an expression, then for. Take the first letter of every word, and a set keeps each letter just once. So you get the unique first letters, in one short line. Wrap it in sorted if you want a stable order for printing. It is that simple. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Unique results in one line.

shorts.title: Keys must be unique
shorts.script: Remember that dictionary keys are unique. In a comprehension, if two items give the same key, the later pair overwrites the earlier one. There is no warning. So when you choose the key, ask yourself, can two items ever give the same key? If so, pick a different key, or a list as the value. Unique keys protect your data, so choose them with care. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Keys are unique.

shorts.title: Lost fish
shorts.script: A quiet bug. You build a dictionary using the first letter of each word as the key. Fish and fig both start with f. The second one overwrites the first. Your dictionary has two pairs, not three, and fish is lost, with no error. Choose a key that is unique, like the whole word, and nothing disappears. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Check your keys.

shorts.hook: "Why did the set comprehension skip the party?"
shorts.script: Why did the set comprehension skip the party? It heard that every item repeats. Your challenge. In one line, build a dictionary that maps the numbers one to five to their squares. Print it. You see one maps to one, two maps to four, up to five maps to twenty five. Use a dictionary comprehension. Share your line in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 38.
